regions.label: text
regions.text: I should like to pose two questions to Mlle Hersch on the methodology of history.
regions.change_reason: Corrected broken word and OCR errors

regions.label: list_item
regions.text: (1) What is her view of « race memory » theories? We agree that the historical situation is concrete and must be known as such. This has tempted people to speak of history as memory. But is it the memory of the race remembering the past, or « collective memory »? This seems to me more dangerous since a race is an abstraction at least in this sense that it does not remember concretely.
regions.change_reason: Corrected text content to match full paragraph structure in image

regions.label: list_item
regions.text: (2) Could Mlle Hersch develop her view about the place of law in historical methodology? Historical thinking is clearly inductive in some sense, though also concrete. But in what sense is it inductive? Surely this is not the induction of the logical textbook?
regions.change_reason: Corrected text content to match full paragraph structure in image

regions.label: text
regions.text: I agree with Mlle Hersch's approach to the extent that she defines historical knowledge by way of the historical object, as reality in the past. Thus her view looks towards the object and not towards the medium of knowledge, like « Verstehen » or R. G. Collingwood's « re-enactment ».
regions.change_reason: Corrected OCR errors and restored full text content

regions.label: text
regions.text: But I wonder whether this ontological position of the past is a sufficient characteristic. The past is a historical past if it has a meaningful position for the present, and mainly if it is the cause of the present. The meaningful aspect and the temporal merge for historical knowledge.
